steps.tx: A reactive **leukocytosis** is defined as an increase in total circulating white blood cell count above eleven thousand per microliter. It represents a coordinated immunological response to infectious, inflammatory, or tissue-destructive insults. The differential leukocyte count identifies the specific lineage involved, categorizing the elevation into neutrophilia, lymphocytosis, monocytosis, eosinophilia, or basophilia based on cytokine signalling.
steps.say: Leukocytosis means a total white blood cell count exceeding eleven thousand per microliter. It reflects the bone marrow response to infection, inflammation, or tissue damage. Breaking down the differential count into neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, or eosinophils points straight to the underlying cause.

vis.title: Patterns and Etiologies of Reactive Leukocytosis
rows: Acute bacterial infection, tissue infarction, burns
Allergies, asthma, invasive parasites, drug reactions

steps.tx: Severe bacterial infections stimulate accelerated bone marrow granulopoiesis, causing immature granulocytes and distinctive cytoplasmic alterations to enter peripheral circulation. Examination of the **reactive toxic granulation** film reveals coarse dark-blue granules in neutrophil cytoplasm, accompanied by pale-blue cytoplasmic Döhle bodies representing aggregated rough endoplasmic reticulum and cytoplasmic vacuolation reflecting active phagocytosis.
steps.say: Reactive toxic granulation on peripheral blood smear demonstrates coarse cytoplasmic granules, Döhle bodies, and vacuolation during acute bacterial infection.

vis.alt: Smear with marked toxic granulation in neutrophils and band forms beside Monospot test.
vis.caption: Smear with marked toxic granulation in neutrophils and band forms beside Monospot test. Toxic granulation, Dohle bodies and monospot panel. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Under acute inflammatory stress, toxic changes emerge in circulating polymorphonuclear neutrophils. The bone marrow accelerates granulopoiesis, discharging band forms and metamyelocytes into blood, creating a **left shift**. Neutrophils display coarse, blue-purple azurophilic primary granules termed toxic granulation, pale blue cytoplasmic inclusions of rough endoplasmic reticulum known as Dohle bodies, and cytoplasmic vacuoles reflecting active bacterial phagocytosis.
steps.say: Severe infection induces a left shift, releasing immature band cells and metamyelocytes. Inside the neutrophils, look for three classic toxic changes: coarse dark purple toxic granules, pale sky-blue patches of rough endoplasmic reticulum called Dohle bodies, and clear vacuoles from active phagocytosis.

left.title: Toxic Cytoplasmic Changes
points: Toxic granulation: coarse primary azurophilic granules
Dohle bodies: light blue rough endoplasmic reticulum
Left shift: band forms exceeding 10 percent

right.title: Normal Neutrophil Morphology
points: Clear, uniform pink cytoplasm without vacuoles
Three to four distinct nuclear lobes

steps.tx: A critical diagnostic challenge is differentiating a benign **leukaemoid reaction** from chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML). A leukaemoid reaction represents an exaggerated reactive response where total leukocyte counts exceed fifty thousand per microliter with abundant immature myeloid precursors. Unlike CML, the leukaemoid state is triggered by severe sepsis or carcinoma, displays prominent toxic granulation, and lacks circulating basophilia.
steps.say: A leukaemoid reaction is an extreme reactive leukocytosis exceeding fifty thousand cells per microliter mimicking leukaemia. Differentiating it from chronic myeloid leukaemia is vital. Leukaemoid reactions occur in severe sepsis, show toxic granules, and lack basophilia, whereas CML is a clonal malignancy with abundant basophils and splenomegaly.

vis.title: Leukaemoid Reaction versus Chronic Myeloid Leukaemia

steps.tx: The biochemical discriminator is the **leukocyte alkaline phosphatase** (LAP) score, evaluated by cytochemical staining of peripheral neutrophils. Normal LAP scores range from twenty to one hundred. In reactive leukaemoid states, active inflammatory cytokines stimulate abundant alkaline phosphatase synthesis, driving the LAP score well above one hundred. In contrast, neoplastic granulocytes in chronic myeloid leukaemia are enzymatically deficient, yielding a low or zero score.
steps.say: The leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score cleanly separates the two. Neutrophils are scored for alkaline phosphatase enzyme activity. In a benign leukaemoid reaction, toxic neutrophils are packed with enzyme, driving the LAP score over one hundred. In CML, neoplastic granulocytes lack the enzyme, dropping the LAP score under twenty.

steps.tx: Reactive viral infections, notably Epstein-Barr virus infectious mononucleosis, elicit striking **atypical lymphocytosis** rather than neutrophilia. CD8-positive cytotoxic T cells become activated against EBV-infected B cells, transforming into Downey cells. These atypical lymphocytes are enlarged with copious, pliable pale-blue cytoplasm that indents and conforms around adjacent red blood cells, exhibiting deep blue basophilia along their scalloped borders.
steps.say: Viral infections like infectious mononucleosis produce atypical lymphocytosis. Activated CD8 cytotoxic T cells, known as Downey cells, expand in response to EBV-infected B cells. These large lymphocytes have flowing pale blue cytoplasm that scallops and indents around neighbouring red blood cells.

vis.title: Atypical Lymphocytes (Downey Cells)
rows: Clonal blast precursors (B, T, or myeloid)

steps.tx: Peripheral blood examination in acute Epstein-Barr virus mononucleosis reveals a profound polyclonal expansion of reactive cytotoxic T lymphocytes. These **Downey atypical lymphocytes** exhibit abundant, pliable cytoplasm that indents and conforms against surrounding erythrocytes, with dark blue peripheral basophilia. Heterophile antibody testing using the rapid latex agglutination Monospot assay confirms the clinical diagnosis.
steps.say: Downey atypical lymphocytes on peripheral blood smear show indented, pliable cytoplasm and confirm reactive lymphocytosis alongside Monospot testing.

vis.alt: Blood smear with large atypical Downey lymphocytes indenting red cells and Monospot inset.
vis.caption: Blood smear with large atypical Downey lymphocytes indenting red cells and Monospot inset. Smear shows atypical lymphocytes indenting red cells plus Monospot. Illustration: StewardMD original.

quiz.q: Which laboratory finding distinguishes a benign leukaemoid reaction from chronic myeloid leukaemia?
options: Markedly elevated leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score > 100
Presence of the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22)
Complete absence of toxic granulation in neutrophils
quiz.explain: A high LAP score (>100) indicates mature, reactive neutrophils in a leukaemoid reaction, whereas CML granulocytes are enzymatically deficient, yielding a low LAP score (<20).

quiz.q: What morphological feature characterizes the atypical lymphocytes (Downey cells) in infectious mononucleosis?
options: Abundant pliable cytoplasm that scallops around adjacent red blood cells
Multiple Auer rods stacked in the cytoplasm
Hypersegmented nuclei containing six or more nuclear lobes
Deeply clefted buttock cell nuclear cleavages
quiz.explain: Atypical lymphocytes in EBV mononucleosis are large activated CD8+ T cells with copious, soft cytoplasm that indents and conforms around neighbouring erythrocytes.
